newsitem.title: EGYPT: Sudanese opposition groups combine military forces.
newsitem.headline: Sudanese opposition groups combine military forces.

text.p: The two wings of the military opposition to the Sudanese government have joined forces close to the Ethiopian border in a significant stepping up of the struggle for power in Africa's largest country.

The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) and the forces of the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) made coordinated attacks on Sunday in Blue Nile province about 600 km (370 miles) southeast of the capital Khartoum.
The SPLA is the largest group of southern rebels. The NDA is an umbrella opposition group including the SPLA but its military forces are mainly northerners based in Eritrea.
"It is the first big combined operation," said Farouq Abu Eissa, the Cairo-based spokesman for the NDA. "It is a big blow to the regime, which is in a panic."
The Sudanese government blamed Ethiopian forces for an attack on the southern part of the front and did not mention the NDA report that it had attacked just to the north.
But President Omar Hassan al-Bashir, in an indication that his Islamist-dominated government took the attacks seriously, called for a "general mobilisation" to hit back.

Diplomats in Cairo said the surprising element was the presence of NDA forces so far south. They have previously carried out only hit-and-run operations further north from across the border from Eritrea, where they have military bases.

On Sunday rebel spokesman Said Arman said NDA and SPLA forces jointly captured the army garrisons at Yakru, Agtura and Manssa in northern Blue Nile. "Those forces managed to destroy four Sudan army brigades," he added.

The SPLA, a southern rebel group fighting the Sudanese government since 1983, has operated before in Blue Nile province. Kurmuk, one of the border towns it says it captured on Sunday, was in SPLA hands for several months from October 1989.
"It's a surprise that the NDA is in that area. It's a new area for them as far I know," one diplomat said.
But Abu Eissa said that Blue Nile province was where the NDA had its largest concentration of forces and that it already controlled large parts of the countryside.
He denied the obvious implication that the Ethiopian government has reactivated its support for Sudanese rebel groups after years of watching from the sidelines.
Ethiopian Marxist ruler Mengistu Haile Mariam, who was overthrown in 1991, openly backed the SPLA for many years.

His successors were initially friendly towards Khartoum but have become increasingly hostile, especially after Egyptian Islamists tried to kill Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995, allegedly with Sudanese help.
"It's not true the NDA has facilities from Ethiopia. The fighting is inside Sudan, deep inside Sudan," Abu Eissa said.
But a statement from the Sudanese armed forces command said Ethiopian forces had shelled Kurmuk and Qassein, another border town about 60 km (35 miles) northeast.

"At three p.m. (1300 GMT) Ethiopian forces along with some of the remnants of agents and mercenaries launched an attack on the said positions and the fighting continued until seven p.m. (1700 GMT) on Sunday," the statement said.
"The armed forces heroically confronted the enemy and inflicted heavy losses on them," it added.
Arman told Reuters in Asmara that SPLA forces were advancing towards Damazin, a large town and the site of Sudan's largest hydroelectric power station.
But Abu Eissa said the plan was not to march on to the capital Khartoum and overthrow the government by military means.
"It has never been our purpose to invade Khartoum. The operations are to detract and weaken the NIF (National Islamic Front) government so the uprising can take place," he said.

Opposition leader Sadeq al-Mahdi, the democratically elected prime minister overthrown by Bashir in 1989, also said this month he still believed that change would come through an uprising, rather than from military action from abroad.
